newsitem.title: USA: Composer Lloyd Webber countersues over copyright.
newsitem.headline: Composer Lloyd Webber countersues over copyright.

text.p: Six years after he was sued for allegedly stealing a Catholic folk musican's work to write the theme to "Phantom of the Opera," composer Andrew Lloyd Webber sent his legal team to court on Monday to countersue.
Ray Repp, who developed the Catholic guitar mass, sued Webber claiming that the theme from the 1987 musical "Phantom of the Opera" was illegally copied from his 1978 religious song "Till You."

U.S. District Court Judge Shirley Kram dismissed Repp's case without bringing it to trial. She ruled that Repp could not prove the songs were sufficiently similar or that Webber had access to Repp's work.

Webber, meanwhile, had filed a counter-claim that any similarity between his and Repp's work was because Repp had copied "Till You" from Webber's 1969 "Close Every Door" from the show "Joseph and the Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat."

Repp's lawyers paint the case as David vs. Goliath, pointing out in testimony that Webber's expert witness, professor Lawrence Ferrara of New York University, had been paid $75,000 for his work on the case.

In court on Monday, Ferrara played bars from the songs on an electric piano and audiotapes and dissected phrases from the songs on giant scores hung on three easels. Court personnel strained to stay awake during the slow testimony with his use of elaborate charts and jargon.

He testified that Repp's 1978 "Till You" and Webber's 1969 "Close Every Door" were "strikingly similar" in structure, melody, rhythm and harmony. He said those songs had more in common than Repp's work and the "Phantom" theme.
While Repp asked for $1 million in punitive damages from Webber, unspecified actual damages and credit for the Phantom theme, Webber's goal in his suit was less clear.
"This case isn't about money. It's about authorship of the music," said Webber's lawyer, Jane Stevens.
She said she was seeking an injunction "preventing his continued exploitation of this work."

"Till You" only ever earned $78.09 and Repp's lawyer, William Coulson, says that it is effectively out of print. He contends the only reason Webber is pressing the case is so that Repp will have a weaker case for an appeal on the "Phantom" song.
He said that Webber's lawyers offered to drop their countersuit if Repp would not appeal.
Both sides expect the trial, which will include more expert forensic musicologists and an appearance by Webber himself, to last until at least Friday.
